items.stimulus:
Although wireless technology dominates everyday experience of the internet, the vast majority of data moving between continents travels not through the air but along the sea floor. Several hundred fibre-optic cables, many of them thousands of kilometres long, link coastlines around the world. In the deep ocean a typical cable is barely thicker than a garden hose, consisting of hair-thin glass fibres wrapped in layers of protective sheathing. Closer to shore, where the risk of damage is greater, cables are given heavier armour and are often buried beneath the sea bed.

Light pulses fade as they travel through glass, so devices called repeaters are spliced into a cable at regular intervals to boost the signal. These repeaters need electricity, which is supplied by a copper conductor running along the cable from stations on land. Satellites can also carry international traffic, but they handle only a small share, partly because they offer far less capacity than a single modern cable.

Cables are surprisingly vulnerable. Each year there are well over a hundred faults worldwide, and most are caused not by natural events or deliberate sabotage but by ordinary human activity at sea, chiefly fishing gear and ships' anchors dragged across the bottom. When a cable breaks, a specialised repair ship is sent to the site. Its crew must lift the damaged ends to the surface, join in a new section and lower the repaired cable back down, a process that can take days or weeks depending on the weather and the depth. To limit the impact of such outages, operators spread traffic over several separate cables, so that the loss of one rarely cuts a country off entirely.

items.stimulus:
When a fishing ground is open to anyone, each boat has a reason to catch as much as it can. A fish left in the water today is not saved for the crew that spared it; it is likely to be taken by a rival tomorrow. Every crew may understand that the stock is shrinking, yet none gains by holding back alone. The idea that shared resources tend to be overused in this way became widely known as the 'tragedy of the commons' after an influential 1968 essay by the ecologist Garrett Hardin. The collapse of Newfoundland's cod fishery, which led Canada to impose a moratorium in 1992, is often cited as a warning.

The simplest response is to set a total allowable catch for each season. Yet a cap on its own can produce a different kind of waste. If the total is shared on a first-come basis, boats race to land fish before the limit is reached, spending heavily on larger engines and putting to sea in dangerous weather. In some fisheries managed this way, the season shrank to a few days, and much of the catch reached the market at once, depressing prices.

A widely adopted alternative divides the total catch into individual shares that holders keep from year to year and, in many schemes, may buy and sell. New Zealand introduced such a system across its main commercial fisheries in 1986, and other countries have since followed. Because a share is worth more when the stock is healthy, holders gain a reason to support cautious limits, and the race to fish disappears because each boat's portion is already guaranteed.

Such schemes are not free of problems. Shares have tended to concentrate in fewer hands, sometimes hurting small coastal towns, and quotas protect fish only if catches are accurately recorded; unwanted fish thrown back dead at sea do not appear in landing figures. In my view, the lesson is not that private shares alone solve the commons problem, but that any limit succeeds only when those who fish have a lasting stake in the stock and monitoring is strong enough to make cheating unprofitable.

items.stimulus:
That many migratory birds can detect the Earth's magnetic field has been accepted for decades, ever since experiments in the 1960s and 1970s showed caged songbirds changing the direction of their restless hopping when the surrounding field was altered. How they detect it remains disputed, and two broad explanations have dominated the debate.

The first proposes that birds carry tiny particles of magnetite, an iron-rich mineral, which would twist or pull in response to the field and so stimulate nearby nerve endings. Early anatomical work reported clusters of iron-containing cells in the upper beaks of pigeons, which seemed to support the idea. Later, more careful studies found that many of these cells were immune cells rather than nerve cells, weakening that line of evidence, though not ruling out magnetite receptors elsewhere in the body.

The second explanation locates the sense in the eye. On this view, light striking certain proteins in the retina triggers a chemical reaction whose outcome depends slightly on the orientation of the magnetic field, so that a bird might in effect see the field as a pattern laid over its vision. Several observations fit this proposal. The birds' compass appears to depend on light of particular wavelengths, and it responds to the angle at which field lines dip towards the ground rather than to whether they point north or south, which is what such a chemical mechanism would predict. Most strikingly, European robins tested in wooden huts on a university campus became disoriented when exposed to weak electromagnetic noise from ordinary electronic equipment, and regained their bearings when the huts were screened. A magnetite particle should be almost unaffected by noise so faint.

Many researchers now suspect that the two explanations are not rivals at all. A bird may use a light-dependent compass in the eye to tell direction while relying on a separate system, perhaps involving magnetite and a nerve running from the beak, to judge its position, much as a navigator needs both a compass and a map. Settling the matter will require identifying the receptor cells themselves, something no laboratory has yet done conclusively.

That many of the cells were immune cells rather than nerve cells

That many migratory birds can detect the Earth's magnetic field has been accepted for decades, ever since experiments in the 1960s and 1970s showed caged songbirds changing the direction of their restless hopping when the surrounding field was altered. How they detect it remains disputed, and two broad explanations have dominated the debate.

The first proposes that birds carry tiny particles of magnetite, an iron-rich mineral, which would twist or pull in response to the field and so stimulate nearby nerve endings. Early anatomical work reported clusters of iron-containing cells in the upper beaks of pigeons, which seemed to support the idea. Later, more careful studies found that many of these cells were immune cells rather than nerve cells, weakening that line of evidence, though not ruling out magnetite receptors elsewhere in the body.

The second explanation locates the sense in the eye. On this view, light striking certain proteins in the retina triggers a chemical reaction whose outcome depends slightly on the orientation of the magnetic field, so that a bird might in effect see the field as a pattern laid over its vision. Several observations fit this proposal. The birds' compass appears to depend on light of particular wavelengths, and it responds to the angle at which field lines dip towards the ground rather than to whether they point north or south, which is what such a chemical mechanism would predict. Most strikingly, European robins tested in wooden huts on a university campus became disoriented when exposed to weak electromagnetic noise from ordinary electronic equipment, and regained their bearings when the huts were screened. A magnetite particle should be almost unaffected by noise so faint.

Many researchers now suspect that the two explanations are not rivals at all. A bird may use a light-dependent compass in the eye to tell direction while relying on a separate system, perhaps involving magnetite and a nerve running from the beak, to judge its position, much as a navigator needs both a compass and a map. Settling the matter will require identifying the receptor cells themselves, something no laboratory has yet done conclusively.

items.stimulus:
For most of the history of life on Earth, night has been dark apart from the moon and stars, and a large share of animal species are active mainly after sunset. In little more than a century, electric lighting has changed that across much of the inhabited world, and satellite measurements suggest that the lit area of the planet is still growing.

The effects on wildlife are varied. Newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean by crawling towards the brightest part of the horizon, which on an undeveloped beach lies over the water; behind a lit promenade they may head inland instead. Many night-flying insects circle streetlamps until they are exhausted or eaten, and a lamp can draw insects away from the surrounding landscape, where some would otherwise have pollinated plants. Bats respond in contrasting ways: some fast-flying species feed eagerly on the insects gathered around lamps, whereas several slower species avoid lit routes altogether, so a single new light can benefit one species while cutting another off from its feeding grounds. Migrating birds, which often travel at night, can be drawn towards brightly lit buildings and collide with them.

It would be easy to conclude that the only remedy is darkness, and that protecting wildlife is therefore incompatible with safe streets. That conclusion seems to me mistaken. Unlike many forms of pollution, light leaves nothing behind: the moment a lamp is switched off, the lamp's effect on its surroundings ends. Much outdoor light is also wasted, spilling sideways or upwards where nobody needs it. Fittings that direct light only downwards, lamps that dim or switch off late at night when streets are empty, and warmer colours containing less of the blue light to which many insects are especially drawn can each reduce harm without leaving people in the dark. Some cities already ask the owners of tall buildings to turn off decorative lighting during peak migration. The obstacle is rarely technical; it is that light is so often treated as harmless that few people think to ask where it falls.

items.stimulus:
For people living hundreds of kilometres from the nearest hospital, a specialist appointment has traditionally meant a long journey by road or light aircraft, with time off work, travel costs and sometimes several nights away from home. Remote consultation is not a new idea: in outback Australia, two-way radio was used to give medical advice to isolated properties for much of the twentieth century. What has changed is the range of care that can now be delivered from a distance. With a reliable connection, a patient in a small clinic can be seen by video by a specialist in a city, while a local nurse or health worker sits alongside to take measurements and carry out simple checks that the specialist requests.

Supporters point out that such appointments are particularly well suited to follow-up visits, in which a doctor reviews the progress of a patient who has already been diagnosed, and to services such as mental health care, where conversation is the main tool. They also argue that care delivered closer to home makes it easier for patients to keep family and cultural ties during treatment.

Telehealth nonetheless has limits. Some conditions cannot be assessed without a hands-on examination or tests requiring equipment that small clinics lack, and a video call can drop out or freeze where internet services are weak, which is often the case in exactly the places that stand to gain most. There is also a concern that if remote consultations simply replace visiting specialists, local staff will lose opportunities to learn from them face to face. For these reasons, many health services treat telehealth as one part of a mixed model, combining video appointments with periodic visits by specialists and with travel to a city hospital when it cannot be avoided. The aim, as they describe it, is not to eliminate travel but to ensure that each journey a patient makes is genuinely necessary.

items.stimulus:
Most people tell small untruths to protect others' feelings: praising a present they dislike, or assuring a nervous friend that an ordinary speech went well. Such lies are usually treated as harmless, even kind. Yet there are reasons to doubt that they are as innocent as they appear.

One objection concerns trust. Praise is valuable only because it is believed, and it is believed only because speakers usually mean it. Each comforting falsehood draws on that shared credit while adding nothing to it. Someone known to praise everything soon finds that their compliments carry no weight, so that when they genuinely admire something they cannot easily say so. A second objection is that kind lies can deprive people of information they need. A friend told that her business plan is excellent may invest her savings in it; a polite lie at the outset can lead to a much greater hurt later.

Defenders of such lies reply that these objections apply mainly to matters of consequence. Nobody's plans depend on whether a host's soup was delicious, and insisting on candour in such moments may express self-regard more than respect for truth. On this view, the morally relevant question is not whether a statement is literally false but whether it serves or betrays the interests of the person who hears it.

This reply seems to me partly right but too quick. It is true that some untruths do no harm, but the speaker is rarely the best judge of which ones those are, since the comforting answer is also the one that spares the speaker an awkward conversation. Moreover, the choice is seldom between a lie and a wounding truth. Between praising a speech and calling it dull lie many honest options: thanking the speaker for their effort, mentioning a passage that did work, or asking how they felt it went. These responses take more thought than a reflexive compliment, which may be precisely why they are less often given. The real failing in most kind lies, then, is not cruelty avoided but effort avoided.

items.stimulus:
An ombudsman is an independent official who investigates complaints from members of the public about the way they have been treated by government bodies. The modern office is usually traced to Sweden, which created a parliamentary ombudsman in 1809, and the word itself comes from a Swedish term for a representative or agent. The idea spread widely in the second half of the twentieth century, and today many countries, as well as regional governments and some industries, have offices of this kind.

An ombudsman is not a court. In most systems the office cannot overturn a decision or order an agency to pay compensation; instead it investigates, reaches findings and makes recommendations. This might seem to leave it toothless, yet agencies accept the great majority of recommendations, partly because an ombudsman can report publicly, and to parliament, on cases where its advice has been ignored. The prospect of such a report is often enough to prompt a change.

Ombudsmen also differ from courts in how they are used. Complaining is normally free, no lawyer is needed, and investigators can examine an agency's files directly rather than relying on what each side chooses to present. Most offices expect complainants to raise the matter with the agency first, stepping in only if that fails. Many can also begin investigations on their own initiative when a pattern of complaints points to a wider problem.

items.stimulus:
A common assumption among hearing people is that sign languages are either a universal code of gestures or a way of spelling out a spoken language on the hands. Neither is correct. There are well over a hundred distinct sign languages in the world, and they do not map neatly onto spoken ones. American Sign Language, for example, is historically related to French Sign Language and is largely unintelligible to users of British Sign Language, even though English is the main spoken language in both countries. Australia's sign language, Auslan, by contrast, belongs to the same family as British Sign Language.

Linguists began to treat sign languages as languages in their own right in the second half of the twentieth century, when researchers showed that signs are built from a limited set of smaller units, such as the shape of the hand, its location and its movement, much as spoken words are built from a limited set of sounds. Changing one of these units can change a sign's meaning. Sign languages also have their own grammar. Signers can place people or objects at points in the space in front of them and then refer back to them by pointing or by directing a verb's movement between those points, and facial expressions such as raised eyebrows can mark a sentence as a question rather than merely conveying emotion.

Further evidence comes from how sign languages are acquired and how they arise. Deaf children exposed to sign from birth pass through stages broadly similar to those of hearing children learning speech, including a phase of repetitive hand movements resembling babbling. When deaf children with no shared language were brought together in new schools in Nicaragua in the late twentieth century, they developed a sign language of their own, which younger pupils arriving later made more systematic. Studies of signers who have had strokes point the same way: damage to left-brain areas important for spoken language tends to disrupt signing too. Fingerspelling, in which letters of a written alphabet are shown by handshapes, does exist, but it is used mainly for names and borrowed words rather than forming the core of the language.

items.stimulus:
In the tragedies performed at Athens in the fifth century BC, the chorus was not a decorative extra but a central element of the performance. Its members, all masked, sang and danced in the orchestra, the circular space between the audience and the stage building, while a small number of actors carried the spoken scenes. The chorus usually represented a group with a stake in the events, such as the elders of a city or the women of a household, and in its songs it might comment on the action, recall earlier events or reflect on the gods and human fortune.

Ancient tradition held that tragedy grew out of choral song, with spoken roles added later. Aeschylus is credited with introducing a second actor and Sophocles a third, and as the number of actors grew, the share of each play given to dialogue increased. The chorus nevertheless remained in view for most of the performance. Its members were ordinary citizens rather than professionals, and the cost of training and costuming them was met by a wealthy citizen appointed to the task, a form of public service that brought prestige.

Modern audiences often find the chorus the hardest part of Greek tragedy to accept. Productions today frequently reduce it to a single speaker or cut its songs, partly because the music and dance that accompanied the words are almost entirely lost. Yet without the chorus, the plays lose the sense that the private suffering of their heroes takes place before a watching community.

The chorus usually represented a group with a stake in the events, such as the elders of a city or the women of a household, and in its songs it might comment on the action, recall earlier events or reflect on the gods and human fortune.

Ancient tradition held that tragedy grew out of choral song, with spoken roles added later. Aeschylus is credited with introducing a second actor and Sophocles a third, and as the number of actors grew, the share of each play given to dialogue increased. The chorus nevertheless remained in view for most of the performance. Its members were ordinary citizens rather than professionals, and the cost of training and costuming them was met by a wealthy citizen appointed to the task, a form of public service that brought prestige.

Modern audiences often find the chorus the hardest part of Greek tragedy to accept. Productions today frequently reduce it to a single speaker or cut its songs, partly because the music and dance that accompanied the words are almost entirely lost. Yet without the chorus, the plays lose the sense that the private suffering of their heroes takes place before a watching community.
